short: Used in three senses: a delivered drive, the physiological change it causes, and the endogenous transmitter class. This volume means the first two.
An endogenous substance that changes neurons' intrinsic firing properties and effective synaptic strengths, and so reconfigures a circuit.
The delivered electrical or magnetic act, as distinct from the modulation it aims to produce; the two words are used interchangeably in the source documents.
The first link of the volume's chain: what is delivered to the organism, whether device current, field, pressure, light or molecule.
The volume's organising sequence: drive → coupling → cellular → subcellular/molecular → circuit → system → outcome.
A commitment that an explanation must link physical scales rather than stay at one; each link names a scale and a kind of entity.
The physical or chemical event by which a delivered drive first changes excitable tissue — the join between drive and cellular response.
What the experimenter set: device parameters, or administered amount and route. Distinguished from what actually acted on tissue.
What actually acted on the tissue: the field at the neuron, the pressure at the transducing cell, the drug concentration at the receptor.
Used two ways: the device-side parameter set an operator controls, and the field or exposure delivered in tissue. This volume means the first.
The in-tissue quantity a drive produces: field at the neuron, in situ acoustic value, or concentration at the receptor.
The named list of parameters, each with unit and provenance, that constitutes a dose for one drive class; a missing value is recorded as missing.
A drug programme must show exposure at the target site, target binding, and expression of pharmacological activity — separately.
Evidence that the drive reached and changed its intended target, shown before any claim that it changed an outcome.
The driving term for extracellular excitation: the second spatial derivative of extracellular potential along a fibre.
A neuron represented as a chain of electrical compartments, each with its own membrane equation, coupled by axial resistance.
A cable model built on a reconstructed three-dimensional dendritic and axonal geometry, used to predict which element a field activates first.
The periodic unmyelinated gap in a myelinated axon where sodium channels cluster and where a cable model places its compartments.
An axon insulated by myelin; in the stimulation literature the element with the lowest threshold to an applied extracellular current.
The threshold current needed to excite an element as a function of its distance from the electrode.
The pulse width at which threshold is twice the value reached with an infinitely long pulse; used to infer which element is being excited.
The sequence in which elements are activated as intensity rises; for applied fields it inverts the physiological order, large fibres first.
Current delivered with the active electrode as cathode; for myelinated fibres usually the lower-threshold polarity, and at the scalp the excitability-lowering one.
Current delivered with the active electrode as anode; at the scalp the polarity conventionally read as raising motor cortical excitability.
Which electrode is anode and which cathode, or the sign of a monophasic phase; a dose parameter that can set the sign of the effect.
The charge delivered in one phase of a stimulus pulse; with charge density, one of the two quantities classical safety limits are written in.
Charge delivered per unit electrode area per phase; with charge per phase, the quantity classical implant safety limits are written in.
A log-linear boundary between safe and damaging combinations of charge per phase and charge density, with a parameter k; widely used as a macroelectrode design rule.
The exposure boundary above which stimulation injures tissue; for electrodes defined jointly by charge and charge density, and contested in scope.
The boundary where current crosses from metal to tissue, by Faradaic or non-Faradaic mechanisms; it sets charge-balance and material limits.
Charge crossing the electrode interface by electrochemical reaction rather than by capacitive charging of the double layer.
A stimulus whose phases deliver equal and opposite charge, so no net charge accumulates at the electrode.
Suppression of action-potential propagation by an applied current, rather than excitation; achievable with strong cathodal or kilohertz-frequency drive.
The non-conducting state voltage-gated sodium channels enter after or without opening; the mechanism modelled for kilohertz conduction block.
A field whose magnitude and direction are effectively constant across a single neuron, as transcranial methods produce.
How much membrane polarisation a unit applied field produces; about 0.12 mV per mV/mm at the soma of rat CA1 pyramidal cells.
The long axis running from a neuron's soma through its dendritic tree; the field component along it sets somatic polarisation.
The opposite-sign polarisation of a neuron's ends in one field: the field that depolarises the soma hyperpolarises the distal dendrite.
Polarisation concentrated where fibre geometry breaks — terminations, bends and gradient changes — which cable analysis predicts dominates in a uniform field.
Whether a field changed the firing of an already-active cell or excited a silent one; the two have very different thresholds.
The electric field a brain generates during its own activity; about 2–4 mV/mm in ferret cortex, used as the yardstick for applied fields.
Amplification of a weak periodic drive when its frequency matches a network's intrinsic rhythm.
Used two ways: a driven evoked response following the stimulus, and engagement of an endogenous rhythm. The 40 Hz and tACS disputes turn on which is scored.
A consistent relationship between spike or oscillation phase and a reference rhythm; the usual measure of entrainment without a rate change.
Volts per metre, the SI unit of electric field strength; 1 V/m equals 1 mV/mm.
Millivolts per millimetre, the field unit used in slice and intracranial work; numerically equal to V/m.
The field injected (tES) or induced (TMS) in tissue; the quantity through which both are assumed to act, and the object of dosimetry.
Estimating the exposure a drive produces in tissue — modelled fields for electromagnetic drives, in situ estimates for ultrasound, fluence at depth for light.
A numerical model of a person's head from MRI, used to estimate the field a montage or coil produces in their brain.
An open pipeline for simulating transcranial magnetic and electric stimulation fields from individual MRI.
The electrical conductivity assigned to each modelled tissue; calibrating it improved agreement with intracranial field measurements.
Loss of applied current through scalp and skull before it reaches the brain; about 75% of scalp-applied current in rodent and human measurements.
The rule for reducing a modelled field to a number; a review of 202 studies found 308 different ones, poorly correlated with each other.
The minimum TMS intensity that reliably elicits a motor response; the clinical norm for dosing, expressed as a percentage.
The constraint that reaching deeper tissue with a non-invasive field means stimulating a larger volume.
A TMS coil of two adjacent windings whose fields sum under the centre, giving more focal stimulation than a circular coil.
A pulsed magnetic field applied outside the head that induces an electric field in cortex, acting mainly on superficial gyral axons.
Trains of TMS pulses delivered to produce effects that outlast the stimulation; graded level A for depression and neuropathic pain.
Low-intensity current applied through scalp electrodes; the family covering tDCS, tACS, tRNS and related waveforms.
Sustained low-intensity direct current at the scalp; its after-effect is read as polarity-specific excitability change, and that reading is disputed.
Sinusoidal current at the scalp, intended to entrain ongoing oscillations; its route in humans at 1–2 mA is disputed.
Scalp current with a noise waveform; in this volume it appears only inside a pooled tES safety envelope.
Two kilohertz carriers at slightly different frequencies whose overlap produces a low-frequency envelope, proposed as a way to reach deep targets non-invasively.
The slow outline traced by a fast carrier's amplitude; the proposed effective stimulus in temporal interference and the culprit in ultrasound's auditory confound.
Asymmetric conversion of an oscillating input into a net directional effect; the mechanism by which a membrane could follow a kilohertz envelope.
Bursts of high-frequency TMS pulses repeated at a theta rhythm; 20–190 s changes motor cortical excitability, with direction set by the pattern.
Theta-burst delivered in short trains separated by pauses; conventionally facilitatory, and the clinical form used in depression protocols.
Theta-burst delivered as one uninterrupted train; conventionally suppressive of motor evoked potentials.
The 600-pulse intermittent theta-burst protocol used clinically; applied to mouse organotypic slices it produced synaptic potentiation with spine remodelling.
Peripheral nerve stimulation paired with a TMS pulse at a fixed interval; the first human protocol written on a Hebbian timing rule.
Applying one stimulation protocol before another so that the prior state sets the sign of the second protocol's effect.
The dependence of a drive's effect on the activation state of the targeted neurons at the moment of delivery.
Delivering stimulation at a chosen phase of an ongoing rhythm, using millisecond-latency real-time EEG.
The 8–13 Hz sensorimotor oscillation whose phase indexes corticospinal excitability in phase-triggered TMS work.
The muscle response to a single stimulation pulse, recorded by EMG; the workhorse readout of human stimulation studies.
Indirect, trans-synaptically generated descending corticospinal volleys, as opposed to the direct D-wave; their recruitment depends on current direction.
The EEG response to a TMS pulse; how much of it is transcranial rather than sensory is disputed.
Recording EEG during TMS to read cortical responses directly; governed by consensus recommendations on recording, artefact correction and interpretation.
Focused, pulsed pressure waves delivered through the skull at intensities below ablation, intended to modulate neural activity focally and deeply.
One episode of ultrasound exposure; its duration is a dose parameter that predicted the direction of human effects.
The fraction of time a pulsed stimulus is on; an acoustic dose parameter whose role in setting the direction of effect is disputed.
How long one stimulus phase lasts; with amplitude it sets charge per phase, and it selects which neural element is recruited.
How often pulses are delivered; in vagal stimulation it set burst timing rather than total activity, and in DBS it is the parameter clinical benefit requires.
A grouped run of pulses; train duration and inter-train interval are dose parameters in their own right.
What a transducer emits into water, measured without the skull; one of the two exposure values every ultrasound study must report.
The estimated acoustic exposure in the brain after transmission through the skull; estimated rather than measured in human work.
Spatial-peak pulse-average acoustic intensity, in W/cm²; the headline ultrasound intensity figure, which alone did not predict direction of effect.
Watts per square centimetre, the unit of acoustic intensity; oocyte channel modulation was reported at 0.3–4.9 W/cm².
Megapascals, the unit of acoustic pressure; barrier opening in rats occurred at a mean peak pressure of 0.28 ± 0.05 MPa.
A dimensionless index of an acoustic field's capacity for mechanical bioeffects; consensus classes ultrasound at MI ≤ 1.9 as non-significant risk.
Thermal dose expressed as the equivalent exposure time at 43 °C; the one transferable dose unit in the volume's thermal literature.
Exposure expressed as an equivalent heating history rather than as applied energy; the basis of both ultrasound safety criteria and ablation planning.
The position that low-intensity ultrasound acts by small measured temperature changes rather than by mechanical parameters.
The account in which acoustic pressure separates the leaflets of the lipid bilayer, rectifying the wave into a capacitance change that drives current.
Used two ways: leaflet separation within the lipid bilayer (intramembrane), and oscillation or collapse of gas bubbles in the vasculature (microbubble).
Injected gas-filled bubbles that oscillate under ultrasound; the active agent in barrier opening, and a dose variable in its own right.
Acoustic signal at half-integer multiples of the drive frequency radiated by oscillating microbubbles; used as a feedback signal for dose.
An underwater microphone used to characterise an acoustic field or to listen for microbubble emissions during sonication.
The steady force a sound wave exerts by transferring momentum to tissue; one of the four candidate ultrasound transducing mechanisms.
A CT-derived measure of skull composition that predicts acoustic transmission; it became a patient-selection criterion for focused ultrasound.
Focused ultrasound at ablative thermal dose, used to make an incisionless lesion; the same physical modality that is reversible at low intensity.
Transient increase of barrier permeability by microbubble oscillation under low-pressure ultrasound, imageable and reversible.
Inflammation triggered by tissue stress rather than infection; reported after microbubble-assisted barrier opening, and disputed as dose-dependent.
Endogenous molecules released by stressed or dying cells that trigger inflammation without a pathogen.
An ion channel gated by membrane force; the protein-based account of how a pressure wave becomes a current.
A mechanically gated cation channel; its conditional deletion in mouse cortex sharply reduced ultrasound-evoked responses.
A TRP-family cation channel proposed as the astrocytic ultrasound transducer, and used as an installed sonogenetic actuator.
An anion channel through which astrocytes are reported to release glutamate after ultrasound-evoked calcium entry.
Two-pore-domain potassium channels whose currents were modulated reversibly by focused ultrasound in oocytes.
A chloride channel that passed outward current under ultrasound in HEK293T cells, extending the candidate transducer list beyond cation channels.
Red to near-infrared light applied to tissue to change cell function; transcranially, its delivered dose is disputed.
Optical energy delivered per unit area, in J/cm²; with irradiance and wavelength, the standard photobiomodulation dose triple.
Optical power delivered per unit area, in mW/cm²; the instantaneous counterpart of fluence.
The fraction of incident light passing through a tissue sample; measured at under 1% through human skull for commercial devices.
Stochastic simulation of photon scattering and absorption through tissue, used to estimate how much light reaches cortex.
The pigment whose concentration strongly attenuates near-infrared light, making skin pigmentation an optical dose covariate.
The terminal enzyme of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, identified as the photoacceptor for red and near-infrared light.
The efficacy of a biological effect plotted against wavelength; used to identify a photoacceptor by matching its absorption spectrum.
A gaseous signalling molecule whose photodissociation from cytochrome c oxidase is the proposed step from light absorption to signalling.
Installing a light-gated protein in chosen cells so that light controls their activity; the field's specificity benchmark.
A light-gated cation channel from algae; it opens within about 1–2 ms and closes within 10–20 ms.
An exogenous protein expressed in chosen cells so that a physical drive has a known coupling target by construction.
Making chosen cells ultrasound-sensitive by expressing a mechanosensitive channel.
The proposal that magnetic fields can gate a ferritin-tethered ion channel; challenged as physically impossible by orders of magnitude.
An iron-storage protein with weak paramagnetism, proposed as the magnetic element in magnetogenetic actuators.
Checking whether a proposed mechanism can supply the energy, force or field the claimed effect requires.
The structure that converts a delivered physical or chemical drive into a change in cell function; a node in the graph, not an edge label.
The fraction of a receptor population bound by a ligand, measured in humans by PET; pharmacology's closest thing to a mechanism-level dose metric.
PET imaging with a reversible D2 ligand, used to measure receptor occupancy and, by competition, endogenous dopamine release.
Imaging the distribution of a radiolabelled tracer in vivo; used here for occupancy, neurotransmitter release, amyloid burden and glial markers.
How tightly a ligand binds its receptor; measured in a dish, it predicts nothing until exposure at the target is measured.
How strongly a bound ligand activates its receptor; the term that must sit beside occupancy for occupancy to predict effect.
A ligand that activates its receptor submaximally however high the occupancy; the counterexample to a universal occupancy window.
A pharmacological framework relating occupancy to response in a functional system through an efficacy parameter.
Action at a site other than the agonist's, changing the receptor's response rather than activating it directly.
A ligand that increases a receptor's response to its agonist without activating it directly; the mechanism of neurosteroid antidepressants.
Where in or on the cell a receptor is engaged; an attribute of the coupling node, because the same agonist acts differently inside and at the surface.
The serotonin receptor subtype through which classic psychedelics act; whether it is necessary for their plasticity effects is disputed.
The endothelial interface controlling entry of molecules into brain tissue by passive diffusion plus active influx and efflux.
The fluid bathing neurons; the concentration there, not in plasma, is the exposure that matters at the receptor.
A compartmental model of drug distribution built from physiology, used to estimate brain target-site exposure when it cannot be measured.
Area under the plasma concentration–time curve; the standard summary of total systemic drug exposure.
The highest plasma concentration reached after a dose; with AUC, the usual summary of exposure.
Relating a measured exposure summary to a clinical endpoint, rather than relating dose to endpoint directly.
How a drug is delivered; a first-class dose variable that fixes onset, exposure profile over time and compartment reached.
The anatomical or cellular space a drive reaches — CSF, parenchyma, plasma, or a subcellular location.
Infusion into the cerebrospinal fluid space through an implanted pump and catheter, placing exposure at the spinal cord.
Driving infusate through brain extracellular space by a sustained pressure gradient, so distribution follows infusion physics rather than diffusion.
Deposition on nasal mucosa, claimed to reach the brain along olfactory and trigeminal routes; the direct fraction is unquantified in humans.
The molecule that actually engages the target, which may be a metabolite of the compound administered.
Expressing an engineered receptor activated only by a designed ligand; slower than optogenetics by about three orders of magnitude.
The ligand designed to be inert for chemogenetics; it does not enter the brain and acts through its conversion to clozapine.
An NMDA receptor antagonist whose single subanaesthetic dose produces antidepressant effects within hours that outlast its clearance.
The S-enantiomer of ketamine, given as a nasal spray; its registration trial adds a blinding problem to the route question.
A ketamine metabolite reported to be antidepressant without NMDA receptor inhibition, and for which no direct target has been found.
Screening a compound against large panels of proteins to identify what it binds; for one ketamine metabolite it found nothing.
A glutamate receptor whose activation gates classical plasticity; also the receptor whose blockade abolishes several human stimulation after-effects.
The glutamate receptor carrying most fast excitatory transmission; its activation was required for a ketamine metabolite's antidepressant-like effect.
The ionotropic inhibitory receptor, target of neurosteroids and anaesthetics acting as allosteric modulators rather than agonists.
The metabotropic inhibitory receptor; the target of baclofen, whose effect depends on which compartment is dosed.
A GABA-B agonist for spasticity; given intrathecally it works in patients in whom the oral route had failed.
Steroids that modulate GABA-A receptors directly and non-genomically, acting either as circulating messengers or as locally synthesised modulators.
An intravenous formulation of allopregnanolone given as a single 60-hour infusion for postpartum depression.
An oral neurosteroid given as 50 mg once daily for 14 days, sharing brexanolone's target pharmacology.
An inhaled anaesthetic gas with antidepressant effect at 25% and 50%, whose benefit emerged weeks after exposure.
Reversible loss of consciousness produced by chemically diverse drugs acting at a small number of molecular targets.
A locally ordered region of the plasma membrane that can host drug binding sites; the pharmacological parallel of membrane-level acoustic coupling.
A 5-HT2A agonist producing altered consciousness and, separately, lasting cortical plasticity; whether the two are linked is disputed.
A psychedelic tryptamine; a single 25 mg dose beat active placebo by 12.3 points on a depression scale in a phase 2 trial.
A psychedelic ergoline; reported to bind TrkB with high affinity at sites partly distinct from the antidepressant site.
A rodent behaviour used as a proxy for the hallucinogenic action of 5-HT2A agonists.
The conscious experience a drug produces; whether it is necessary for a psychedelic's enduring therapeutic effect is disputed.
The dopamine precursor for Parkinson's disease; its clinical problems are attributed to erratic delivery rather than receptor pharmacology.
Whether a receptor population is engaged in peaks or steadily; the two give different long-term outcomes at the same target.
A D2 partial agonist that keeps extrapyramidal risk low at high occupancy, breaking the universal occupancy window.
The dopamine receptor subtype whose occupancy defines the antipsychotic therapeutic window of about 65–80%.
The reuptake transporter targeted by SSRIs; 70–80% occupancy is quoted as the antidepressant window.
The assumption that depression involves lowered serotonin; an umbrella review found the main research areas give it no support.
A lasting increase in synaptic strength after brief patterned input; first shown in anaesthetized rabbit hippocampus.
A lasting decrease in synaptic strength; the negative-direction counterpart of LTP in the borrowed plasticity vocabulary.
A human after-effect resembling LTP in three properties — it follows patterned input, outlasts it, and its sign depends on the pattern — but without a measured synaptic change.
A learning rule in which the sign of a synaptic change depends on postsynaptic activity relative to a threshold set by the neuron's own recent average activity.
A change in a synapse's capacity for later plasticity, without necessarily changing its present strength.
Plasticity that stabilises activity around a set point, lowering the plasticity threshold after activity has been reduced.
Uniform multiplicative adjustment of a neuron's synaptic strengths to stabilise its firing rate, preserving relative weights.
Plasticity whose sign depends on the millisecond order of pre- and postsynaptic spikes; the rule paired associative stimulation was written on.
A neuromodulator whose presence is required for a timing rule to produce plasticity at all.
A brief rise in excitability, attributed to reduced intracortical inhibition, that permits a plasticity effect during practice.
The spread of individual responses to a fixed protocol; in three standard protocols only 39–45% of people moved in the expected direction.
A neurotrophin that is the field's most cited convergence point; a rise in it distinguishes none of the routes that can produce it.
The BDNF receptor, reported as both a downstream requirement for stimulation-induced plasticity and a direct binding target of several drug classes.
A common BDNF variant impairing activity-dependent release; Met carriers respond differently across several stimulation protocols, inconsistently replicated.
A translation-control kinase pathway activated rapidly by ketamine in rat prefrontal cortex, with rapamycin blocking both synaptogenesis and behaviour.
An mTOR inhibitor used as the blocking agent that ties ketamine's synaptogenesis to its behavioural effect in rats.
A translation-elongation kinase whose deactivation after NMDA receptor blockade releases BDNF messenger RNA for translation.
The postsynaptic protrusion holding most excitatory synapses; spine number and remodelling are the structural readouts of rapid plasticity.
A gene transcribed within minutes of neural activity, used as a cheap, anatomically resolved marker that tissue was driven.
The canonical immediate-early gene product, used to mark which regions a stimulus drove.
Genome-wide expression measured with anatomical position retained; the modern high-resolution version of an activity-marker readout.
Respiratory-chain activity and related metabolism; for photobiomodulation the proposed transducer, for other drives a downstream endpoint.
Current per unit area in tissue or at an electrode; one of the parameters the classical charge-density safety rule omits.
The claim that physically unrelated drives meet at the same molecular endpoint; weaker than it looks unless the assay is shared.
A finding not yet reproduced outside the group that proposed it; flagged as such on the edge rather than merged with replicated work.
A glial cell type that responds to direct current on a larger scale than local neurons and is a candidate ultrasound transducer.
The brain's resident immune cells; their state is the contested effector in the 40 Hz amyloid literature.
A mitochondrial protein used as a PET marker of neuroinflammation; it rises in activated mouse microglia but not in primates or human disease.
The astrocytic water channel whose endfoot polarisation is central to glymphatic clearance.
The peptide whose aggregation marks Alzheimer's disease; the endpoint in both the 40 Hz claim and the barrier-opening trial.
Driving the brain at 40 Hz by light or sound, claimed to entrain gamma and reduce amyloid; each link of that chain is separately contested.
Fast (roughly 30–80 Hz) rhythmic population activity; the target of 40 Hz protocols and a control signal in adaptive deep brain stimulation.
Consistent phase alignment between two oscillating populations; in the communication-through-coherence account, the variable that gates routing.
Rhythmic population activity treated in this volume as a control variable rather than a by-product.
The summed extracellular voltage near a recording contact; the signal used as a control variable in adaptive deep brain stimulation.
A transient rise in 13–30 Hz subthalamic activity treated as a pathological marker in Parkinson's disease and used to trigger stimulation.
Chronic pulsed stimulation through an implanted intracranial electrode; how its high-frequency benefit arises is disputed.
The account in which high-frequency stimulation forces output spiking into a regular, variance-free pattern, so the neuron fires but carries no information.
Action potentials travelling backwards along an axon toward the cell body, by which deep stimulation can recruit cortex.
A large, focal ringing response evoked in the subthalamic nucleus by stimulation pulses; used for target verification rather than control.
Deep brain stimulation whose delivery is gated by a recorded neural marker rather than run continuously.
Stimulation whose drive depends on the state it modulates, through a measured control variable and a threshold rule.
A measured signal standing in for a state of interest; in closed loops it both indexes and is shaped by the intervention.
Choosing a stimulation site by its connectivity to a distant region rather than by local anatomy; how much outcome variance it explains is disputed.
Whether a target is the literature coordinate, the coil position, or the tissue a field model says was stimulated; part of the claim, not a detail.
Connectivity averaged over a healthy reference cohort, used to characterise a patient's stimulation volume without patient-specific imaging.
Statistical dependence between regional activity time courses, usually from resting-state fMRI; the basis of connectivity-based targeting.
A ventromedial prefrontal region whose anticorrelation with a prefrontal stimulation site was proposed as a targeting rule for depression.
The standard cortical target for antidepressant stimulation; high-frequency repetitive TMS there is graded definitely effective.
Brainstem and basal-forebrain populations releasing acetylcholine, noradrenaline, dopamine or serotonin broadly; both targets of a drive and gates on its effect.
The pontine noradrenergic nucleus; the best-characterised device-engageable neuromodulator source and the origin of the adaptive-gain account.
The account in which locus coeruleus activity sets neural gain, with phasic responses supporting task engagement and elevated tonic firing favouring exploration.
Brief event-locked bursts against sustained background rate; two regimes of the same nucleus with different functional consequences.
Measuring pupil size as a non-invasive stand-in for noradrenergic engagement; a monotonic but weak and state-dependent proxy.
The basal-forebrain cholinergic source whose lesion abolishes device-driven cortical map plasticity in rats.
Enlargement of a body-part representation in cortex after paired training and stimulation, mapped by intracortical microstimulation.
How a putative requirement was tested — lesion, genetic deletion, receptor antagonism — which the necessity claim must carry.
The transmitter of the efferent anti-inflammatory limb and one of the four plasticity-gating modulators.
A neuromodulator measurable in humans by tracer displacement; prefrontal stimulation released it focally in the ipsilateral dorsal caudate.
The locus coeruleus transmitter; the system most device protocols claim to engage, indexed in humans only by weak proxies.
A neuromodulator and the target of the antidepressant class whose deficit premise an umbrella review found unsupported.
A control procedure meant to reproduce a drive's sensations without its intended effect; different shams deliver different things.
Keeping participants and assessors unaware of allocation; usually judged from end-of-study guesses, which may overestimate how well masking held.
What a participant expects a treatment to do; unreported in most drug trials here, and a route by which unblinding inflates effects.
A control agent that produces noticeable effects of its own, used to make blinding credible when the test drug is unmistakable.
Unintended stimulation of scalp, ear or peripheral nerves accompanying every non-invasive drive; a rival explanation rather than mere noise.
Activation produced through the ear by a stimulus aimed elsewhere; in ultrasound it competes with all four proposed transduction accounts.
The account in which a transcranial effect is produced by stimulating scalp and cervical nerves rather than cortex directly.
A measurable quantity standing in for an inaccessible one; the edge that uses it inherits its validity, which is often weak.
The quantity a study actually measures, usually several levels away from the coupling step it makes claims about.
A dispute treated as a first-class object, with its rival claims attached, each carrying its own species, preparation and evidence kind.
Two edges between the same nodes representing competing explanations rather than duplicate assertions.
The biological system an experiment was run in — culture, slice, anaesthetised animal, awake animal, person — which travels with every claim.
Carrying a result from one species to another; fields do not scale with heads, and markers do not always transfer either.
Genetic deletion of a gene to test necessity; the strongest available evidence for assigning a transducer, and sensitive to where the deletion is made.
Explanted tissue kept in culture with its local circuitry intact, allowing a clinical protocol to be applied where synapses can be measured.
Whether a result recurs on repetition; in a survey of electrical stimulation researchers only about 45–50% said they could routinely reproduce published results.
The intraclass correlation coefficient, used for test–retest reliability; across 15 studies of rTMS after-effects it was 0.29–0.70.
A standardised mean difference corrected for small-sample bias; the effect-size unit used throughout the volume's pooled estimates.
A difference in means divided by a pooled standard deviation; the generic effect size in the volume's meta-analyses.
The ratio of the evidence for two hypotheses; BF10 favours the effect, BF01 the null, so a null can be supported rather than merely unrejected.
Quantitative pooling of studies; a pooled estimate inherits whatever confounds its inputs carried, which the graph should record.
The pre-specified amount by which a new treatment may be worse and still be declared not meaningfully inferior.
The probability of detecting a true effect; low power also lowers the chance a significant result is true and inflates published effect sizes.
A relationship in which effect rises then falls with dose, so the sign or size of an effect cannot be read from amount alone.
A structured multi-round expert consultation used to produce reporting standards where no empirical basis for them exists.
An agreed item list a study should report; the nearest thing to a protocol ontology, supplying items but no identifiers or class hierarchy.
The part of the schema that has to be authored rather than reused, because no ontology in this corpus covers stimulation protocols or device parameters.
A graded statement of how certain an effect is; GRADE rates certainty and recommendation strength separately, while neuromodulation guidelines use letter scales.
A graph whose nodes and edges carry typed key–value properties, so a claim's dose, species and controls can live on the edge.
The relation in a subject–predicate–object statement; the label on an edge, such as delivers, couples_via, activates or modulates.
A compact identifier of the form prefix:local-id, such as UBERON:0000955, by which a node cites the ontology term it means.
A species-neutral anatomy ontology of more than 6,500 classes that links species-specific anatomy ontologies.
The family of interoperable biomedical ontologies from which the schema's cell, molecular and chemical identifiers come.
A community ontology of evidence types, used by dozens of biomedical databases to record how an assertion is supported.
An ontology that names a neuron type by decomposing it into phenotypes carrying identifiers from community ontologies.
A curated, ontology-backed record of the origins, terminations and routing of autonomic projections; the closest existing model for this volume's graph.
A manually curated database representing drug mechanisms as paths through a biomedical knowledge graph; the closest precedent for the volume's shape.
A database of subject–predicate–object predications extracted automatically from PubMed; the alternative acquisition route, and the one the volume distrusts.
An ordered sequence of claim edges from drive to outcome, made first-class so that rival paths between the same endpoints can coexist.
Electrical stimulation of the vagus nerve, usually by an implanted cuff; the volume's best-characterised parametric drive.
The tenth cranial nerve, mostly afferent, carrying molecularly distinct sensory classes as well as parasympathetic efferents.
Non-invasive stimulation at the auricular branch of the vagus; human target engagement is unproven for continuous protocols.
The account in which the nervous system senses and regulates inflammatory state in real time through an afferent, central and efferent cholinergic loop.
The sympathetic nerve to the spleen, whose relay to cytokine-producing cells passes through acetylcholine-making T lymphocytes.
The acetylcholine receptor subtype on cytokine-producing cells through which cholinergic signalling suppresses TNF release.
A pro-inflammatory cytokine; the molecular endpoint that made the neuroimmune chain measurable from drive to outcome.
A transcription factor pathway central to inflammatory gene expression; its activation after barrier opening tracked microbubble dose.
An intestinal epithelial cell that forms a glutamatergic synapse with a vagal afferent, transducing luminal stimuli in milliseconds.
Sensing of the body's internal state, carried largely by vagal and other visceral afferents.
The hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal endocrine cascade; the afferent vagal route to immune control, distinct from the efferent cholinergic one.
The adrenal stress hormone used as an endocrine readout; prefrontal stimulation reduced its acute response to a laboratory stressor.
A transcranial drive under general anaesthesia that induces a generalised seizure; in this corpus reported only by schedule and outcome.
Threshold outcomes on a clinical scale — usually a percentage improvement (response) or falling below a severity cut-off (remission).
Pulsed stimulation in the epidural space over the spinal cord; standard care for chronic pain, with dorsal-root afferents as the first element recruited.
A basal ganglia nucleus and the main deep brain stimulation target in Parkinson's disease.
The large deep-cortical output neuron most sensitive to applied fields in the modelling and slice literature.
The outer bend of a cortical fold, where the induced field is strongest and where TMS is thought to act first.
The exposure range within which a modality has been used without serious harm; wider than the range in which efficacy is certain.
Millijoules per square millimetre, an energy-flux-density unit used for pulsed acoustic devices; this volume's optical and acoustic sources report J/cm² and MPa instead.
Recording muscle electrical activity; the channel through which motor evoked potentials and rodent motor responses are measured.
Using a drug with known receptor action to assign a molecular identity to a stimulation-induced effect; a measurement instrument before a treatment.
